Hands-on Exercise 5a

Visual Correlation Analysis

Author

Jedidiah Asaf T

Overview

This hands-on exercise recreates the key techniques from Chapter 6 of R for Visual Analytics. The focus is on building correlation matrices and corrgrams to reveal the pairwise relationships among the physicochemical properties of wine, using corrplot and ggstatsplot.

Setup

Code 
if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")

pacman::p_load(
  corrplot,
  ggstatsplot,
  tidyverse
)

wine <- read_csv("data/wine_quality.csv")

Data Preview

Code 
DT::datatable(
  head(wine, 50),
  class = "compact",
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
)

1. Building a Correlation Matrix with pairs()

1.1 Basic Scatterplot Matrix

Code 
pairs(wine[, 1:11])

1.2 Lower-corner Only

Showing only the lower half removes the redundant mirror image.

Code 
pairs(wine[, 2:12], upper.panel = NULL)

1.3 Showing the Correlation Coefficient

A custom panel.cor() function prints the absolute correlation in the upper panel, sized by strength.

Code 
panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits = digits)[1]
  txt <- paste0(prefix, txt)
  if (missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8 / strwidth(txt)
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

pairs(wine[, 2:12], upper.panel = panel.cor)

2. Corrgram with ggstatsplot

2.1 ggcorrmat()

ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat() draws the correlation coefficients and marks the statistically non-significant pairs with a cross.

Code 
ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11
)

2.2 Grouped Corrgram by Wine Type

Code 
grouped_ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  grouping.var = type,
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 2)
)

3. Corrgram with corrplot

3.1 Computing and Plotting the Correlation Matrix

Code 
wine.cor <- cor(wine[, 1:11])
corrplot(wine.cor)

3.2 Changing the Visual Element

Using ellipses and showing only the lower half.

Code 
corrplot(
  wine.cor,
  method = "ellipse",
  type = "lower"
)

3.3 Mixed Layout

Ellipses in the lower half, coefficients in the upper half.

Code 
corrplot.mixed(
  wine.cor,
  lower = "ellipse",
  upper = "number",
  tl.pos = "lt",
  diag = "l",
  tl.col = "black"
)

3.4 Combining with a Significance Test

Pairs whose correlation is not significant at the 0.05 level are left blank.

Code 
wine.sig <- cor.mtest(wine[, 1:11], conf.level = 0.95)

corrplot(
  wine.cor,
  method = "number",
  type = "lower",
  diag = FALSE,
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 45,
  p.mat = wine.sig$p,
  sig.level = 0.05
)

3.5 Reordering with Hierarchical Clustering

corrplot can reorder the variables so that strongly correlated groups sit together, with cluster rectangles drawn on top.

Code 
corrplot(
  wine.cor,
  method = "ellipse",
  tl.pos = "lt",
  tl.col = "black",
  order = "hclust",
  hclust.method = "ward.D",
  addrect = 3
)

Learning Reflection

In this exercise, I learned that a correlation matrix is far easier to read as a corrgram than as a table of numbers. pairs() gives a quick raw look, but ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat() adds real value by flagging non-significant relationships, and grouped_ggcorrmat() lets me compare red and white wine side by side. corrplot is the most flexible: reordering by hierarchical clustering and drawing cluster rectangles turned a noisy 11×11 matrix into clear blocks of related chemical properties.
